source.title: Where You Measure Decides What You Measure: Position Selection in Ablation-Based SAE Evaluation

record.tranche_reason: The paper studies position selection in SAE causal-ablation evaluation, not whether neurons or SAE features have coherent or polysemantic meanings. Its results concern a related but different measurement construct.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results about how measurement position changes SAE causal-effect estimates. Those results do not measure polysemanticity, mixed input responses, or whether a unit has one coherent job, so they do not test V1–V7. The five-paper reporting audit and cited results from other work are not study-result rows.
record.test_reason: The paper studies which token position is used when ablating SAE latents to measure causal effect. It never measures whether neurons or latents respond to unrelated inputs, so it bears on no version. Superposition (Elhage et al.) appears only as background for SAEs, and Bolukbasi et al.'s max-activation illusion is only cited. V7 concerns how polysemanticity is judged; this paper's position-selection result concerns causal-effect magnitude, a different construct.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that the dictionary-chosen top-activating position accounts for most of the latent×arm disagreement in zero-ablation magnitude measurements. Fixing a shared position largely removes it; the Gemma-3-1B reduction partly depends on the selection rule. The problem does not shrink with larger evaluation corpora, and positions should be reported.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates SAE causal-ablation measurement conventions, not the original neuron-activation interpretation method.
record.method_sensitivity: Position agreement falls as the evaluation corpus grows. The reduction in latent×arm variance under shared positions depends partly on the shared-position selection rule for gemma-3-1b.

fits_no_version.finding: Top-activating measurement positions chosen by different SAE dictionaries for matched latents agree only 30–48% (released Gemma Scope) and 10–18% (six controlled arms), and agreement falls as the corpus grows. Fixing a shared position cuts latent×arm variance in ablation KL from 7.6%/11.9% to 0.0%/2.4%; part of the Gemma-3-1B reduction depends on the shared-position rule.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Single-latent ablation causal-effect estimates depend on which token position is measured, and that position is selected by the dictionary under evaluation.

record.problems: The main controlled comparison uses two Gemma base models and a retained subset of latents that fire in every arm at a common position. The six SAE arms were trained on 12M tokens, much less than the production dictionaries discussed. The paper reports that one shared-position rule can affect the result for gemma-3-1b, and that smaller-corpus estimates can be clipped to zero. It also states that results are sensitive to evaluation corpus size and that behavior in other architectures is untested.
record.rows_left_out: No additional study results about polysemanticity were reported. The study's other results on intervention normalization, special-token handling, alignment, training contrasts, and propagation concern other evaluation questions and were not included.

untested.parts: Image-classifier neurons responding to unrelated inputs; no vision models studied.
Share of polysemantic MLP neurons in language models and its variation by layer; only residual-stream SAE latents' ablation effects are measured.
Superposition as the cause of polysemanticity; cited as SAE motivation only.
Polysemanticity arising without capacity pressure; not examined.
Architecture, activation or regularization effects on the polysemantic share; the arms vary fitting choices but measure causal-effect variance, not polysemanticity.
Canonical polysemantic units reinterpreted as one shared feature; not examined.
Dependence of polysemanticity judgments on the activation range examined or on explanation scoring; the paper's position dependence concerns ablation KL, not interpretation.

record.verdict_notes: The rows are correctly linked to no version; their states are cannot_determine because none measures polysemanticity. The within-cell position share (67.4%, §5/Appendix F) and the normalisation sign flip (Appendix A) are also off-claim and need no rows. No instructions were found in the text.

versions.untested_parts: Whether image-classifier neurons respond to several unrelated inputs.
Whether a large share of transformer MLP neurons respond to unrelated tokens or contexts, and variation across layers.
Whether superposition or capacity pressure causes polysemanticity.
Whether polysemanticity arises without capacity pressure from initialization, regularization, or training noise.
Whether architecture, activation function, or regularization changes the share of polysemantic neurons, or whether it can be reduced without large performance loss.
Whether canonical polysemantic units actually detect one shared feature or related jobs.
Whether polysemanticity judgments depend on activation-range selection or explanation scoring. The paper tests position selection for SAE causal-ablation measurements instead.
